source: van Eemeren (2023) The Pragma-Dialectical Approach to the Fallacies Revisited (Argumentation)
finding: Authors summarise their 1996-2008 project 'Conceptions of Reasonableness'. Ordinary arguers, with no training, judged discussion moves that break a rule for critical discussion. They rated them unreasonable.
numbers: 24 fallacy types tested. 7-point scale (1 very unreasonable, 4 neutral, 7 very reasonable). All fallacious moves rated below 4 except the tu quoque variant of ad hominem. Non-fallacious look-alikes generally rated reasonable. Difference statistically significant. Table 1 values themselves were an image and not read.
limits: Self-report of the original team, not independent. Rules named as tested: 1 (Freedom), 2 (Obligation to Defend), 8 (Argument Scheme), 9 (Concluding). Clear-cut, unloaded cases only.
agent_relevance: Rule-violation labels line up with lay judgment for clear cases. A rule checklist could be a fair audit lens for a critic step, but this does not show it improves answers.
quote: Fallacious discussion moves are in general considered unreasonable by the respondents and non-fallacious moves are considered reasonable.

source: van Eemeren (2023) The Pragma-Dialectical Approach to the Fallacies Revisited (Argumentation)
finding: Design of the experiments: respondents did not judge the rules abstractly. They judged short two-person dialogues in which one rule was or was not broken.
numbers: Dialogues in domestic, political or scientific settings. Repeated-measures design combined with a multiple-message design (many instances per fallacy plus non-fallacious twins). In some cases a replication was run.
limits: Fragments were short and written by the researchers. Judgments of third-party text, not live argument. Participant numbers per study not given in this review.
agent_relevance: Method worth copying for LLM evaluation: paired fallacious and matched non-fallacious items, many instances, one rule at a time.

source: van Eemeren (2023) The Pragma-Dialectical Approach to the Fallacies Revisited (Argumentation)
finding: Hidden fallaciousness test 1: an abusive ad hominem is judged less unreasonable when it looks like a reaction to someone who wrongly poses as an authority. Hypothesis confirmed in both experiments.
numbers: Two experiments (van Eemeren, Garssen and Meuffels 2012). Direction confirmed in both. Effect sizes not given in this review.
limits: Effect sizes not read. Camouflage works only when a legitimate-looking frame is available.
agent_relevance: Surface framing can hide a rule violation from readers. LLM judges and critics may be fooled the same way. A test case for a critic prompt.

source: van Eemeren (2023) The Pragma-Dialectical Approach to the Fallacies Revisited (Argumentation)
finding: Hidden fallaciousness test 2: an ad baculum threat is rated more reasonable when it can be read as well-meant advice. Same logic tested for ad consequentiam, camouflaged by ambiguous descriptive or prescriptive wording.
numbers: Ad baculum: confirmed (2015 chapter, pages 316-319 cited). Ad consequentiam: an experiment tested that the camouflaged variant is judged less unreasonable than the plain one.
limits: Numbers for ad consequentiam not stated here. Same authors again.
agent_relevance: Ambiguity between two speech acts is the cover. A prompt can ask the model to state which act a move performs before judging it.

source: van Eemeren (2023) The Pragma-Dialectical Approach to the Fallacies Revisited (Argumentation)
finding: The theory says the discussion rules have two kinds of validity: problem-solving validity (argued analytically) and conventional validity (accepted by the people involved, which only experiments can show).
numbers: Project completed 2008. Research question: to what extent the norms arguers claim to use agree with the pragma-dialectical standards.
limits: The experiments test conventional validity only. Problem-solving validity is argued, not measured. No test that following the rules makes disputes end better.
agent_relevance: This gap matters for us. Nobody here measured whether rule-following improves outcomes, which is what an agent scaffold needs.

source: van Eemeren, Garssen, Meuffels (2009) Fallacies and Judgments of Reasonableness (Springer, book page)
finding: Book reports more than ten years of experiments on conventional validity of the rules, with ordinary arguers who had no argumentation training, over a wide range of fallacies.
numbers: 9 chapters: ad hominem as exemplary study, freedom rule, obligation to defend (two chapters), argument scheme rule, concluding rule, conclusion on conventional validity. Springer shows 142 citations.
limits: Paywalled. Only the book page and review blurbs were read, not the chapters.
agent_relevance: Primary evidence base for the lay-validity claim. Result figures must come from the review above.

source: Hample (2010) review of Fallacies and Judgments of Reasonableness, Argumentation 24, as quoted on the Springer book page
finding: An outside reviewer sees consistent evidence for conventional validity of the rules, useful data on lay views of fallacies even without the theory, and a model of programmatic empirical work.
numbers: Qualitative. No numbers in the quoted blurb.
limits: Quoted publisher blurb only. Full review paywalled, so any reservations are not seen. Reviewer says the book has 'varying levels of value to different scholars'.
agent_relevance: Independent endorsement is weak evidence. It is not a replication.
quote: The research program offers consistent evidence for the conventional validity of the discussion rules at the heart of pragma-dialectics.

source: Hornikx (2010) review in Information Design Journal 18(2), as quoted on the Springer book page
finding: Praised as an example of how experimental studies can be built from a normative theory, with a large set of well-designed experiments.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Publisher blurb. Hornikx works on argumentation experiments himself.
agent_relevance: Method lesson: a normative theory can be turned into testable item pairs.

source: van Eemeren, Garssen, Meuffels (2009) Conventional Validity of the Pragma-Dialectical Discussion Rules (book chapter 9)
finding: The summary chapter. Fallacies are treated as moves that hinder or block resolution on the merits (rule violations), not as formally invalid inferences.
numbers: Pages 203-224. Only the opening paragraph was open.
limits: Paywalled. No figures read.
agent_relevance: Useful framing: judge a move by whether it blocks resolution, not by formal validity alone.

source: Independent replication check of the Amsterdam rule-judgment experiments
finding: No independent replication was found in the sources I could reach. The team replicated some of its own tests, per the 2023 review.
numbers: None found.
limits: Absence of evidence under tool limits: OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv search APIs returned 429 and the web search quota was used up. Not proof that no replication exists.
agent_relevance: Treat the lay-validity result as single-lab, with in-house replication.

source: van Eemeren, Meuffels, Verburg (2000) The (Un)Reasonableness of Ad Hominem Fallacies, J. Language and Social Psychology 19(4)
finding: Early experimental test that ad hominem variants are judged unreasonable by lay readers. Located by DOI only. Page was blocked by a bot check.
numbers: Not read, no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Earliest cell of the Amsterdam program, listed so a later pass can open it.

source: van Eemeren, Garssen, Meuffels (2012) The disguised abusive ad hominem empirically investigated, Thinking and Reasoning 18(3)
finding: Journal report of the two ad hominem camouflage experiments summarised in the 2023 review. Full text blocked.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Same as above.

source: Hahn and Oaksford (2007) The rationality of informal argumentation: a Bayesian approach to reasoning fallacies, Psychological Review 114
finding: The main rival to rule-based fallacy theory. As I know it, the view says fallacy-type arguments are strong or weak by degree, depending on probabilities, not by a yes or no rule violation.
numbers: Not read, no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Located via Crossref only. Description is from memory of the field, not from this session's reading.
agent_relevance: A Bayesian check (how much does this reason move belief?) is a rival audit lens that suits a single agent better than a discussion rule list.

source: Coverage check: which rules the reviewed experiments name
finding: The 2023 review names tests of rules 1, 2, 8 and 9 across the four stages. Rules on starting points, unexpressed premises, relevance and validity appear only in its list of newer fallacies, not as tested rules.
numbers: 4 of 10 rules named as tested in the review's Section 2.
limits: Based on the review's wording. The book may test more rules than the review lists.
agent_relevance: Do not claim all ten rules are lay-validated.

source: The Logical Perspective in Pragma-dialectics (Topoi 2024)
finding: Argues the theory does not integrate the logical view of arguments. The Validity Rule and the Argument Scheme Rule are procedural yet behave like logical rules. Three periods are described (conventionalist, inferentialist, dualist) and none is satisfying.
numbers: Qualitative. No experiment.
limits: Philosophical critique, no data.
agent_relevance: Rule-based critique is weakest where it needs a notion of a valid reason. A schema should not lean on PD for argument-level checks.

source: Convincing in Pragma-Dialectics: A Critical Reassessment (Topoi 2024)
finding: Argues the link between arguing and convincing is conceptually unstable. Proposes grounding resolution in speakers' non-verbal contact with evidence instead of only verbal exchange.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Conceptual paper. Says the proposal is compatible with PD if methods are adjusted.
agent_relevance: Rival view: resolution turns on contact with evidence. That matches an agent that can run checks or tools.

source: AI-Authorship Accusations Against Human Discussants: A Pragma-Dialectical Account of Procedural Derailment (Argumentation 2026)
finding: New PD paper on the LLM era. Calling a contribution machine-written is a move in the argumentation stage that shifts the talk from the standpoint to the speaker's status. The authors name this 'procedural capture' and offer a repair protocol with a warrant-filter for detector evidence.
numbers: No data. Worked examples are analytic reconstructions.
limits: Normative, not descriptive.
agent_relevance: Rule worth keeping: do not let source attribution replace argument on the merits. A critic step should not dismiss a claim by its origin.
quote: The claim is normative rather than descriptive: the worked examples are analytic reconstructions.

source: Experimental Insights into the Influence of Logic and Pragmatics on Conditional Argument Evaluation (Argumentation 2026)
finding: Adjacent argumentation experiment from an Amsterdam setting. Pragma violations slowed responses and made invalid conditionals easier to reject, without hurting valid ones. With lever-style wording people rejected more invalid and accepted fewer valid arguments.
numbers: Experiment 1: 25 participants (mean age 23.9, SD 3.6), mostly Amsterdam students, 2 x 2 design. Experiment 2 used Periodic Table of Arguments wording.
limits: Small convenience sample. Not a test of the pragma-dialectical rules, only adjacent.
agent_relevance: Wording shifts validity judgments. Test prompts in more than one wording.

source: Pragma-dialectical perspective to intercultural discussion as communicative activity (Humanities and Social Sciences Communications 2023)
finding: Says the standard model cannot describe discussion across cultures. Adds identification, pragmatic acts, motivation and mediation to it, then checks it in one case study.
numbers: One case study. No sample size or effect size.
limits: Exploratory. Only the abstract was read closely.
agent_relevance: Culture moderator: the rule set grew from a Dutch school and has had little cross-cultural testing.

source: Jin et al. (2022) Logical Fallacy Detection (arXiv 2202.13758)
finding: First broad fallacy-detection set (LOGIC) plus a climate challenge set. A structure-aware classifier beat the best language model it compared.
numbers: LOGIC: 2,449 fallacy examples over 13 types. LOGICCLIMATE: 1,079 samples. Gain of 5.46% F1 on LOGIC and 4.51% on LOGICCLIMATE.
limits: Examples come from quiz websites, so they are textbook-like. Not based on the ten rules. Older models.
agent_relevance: Models can learn textbook fallacy forms. Whether that holds in messy real text is open.

source: Alhindi, Chakrabarty et al. (2022) Multitask Instruction-based Prompting for Fallacy Recognition (arXiv 2301.09992)
finding: Instruction prompting with T5 across datasets covers 28 unique fallacies. Cites the ten rules of a critical discussion as one fallacy typology and notes datasets use between 5 and 18 types.
numbers: Beats single-dataset models by 16% average macro F1, few-shot baselines by 25% and zero-shot by 40%, across five datasets.
limits: Different fallacy lists per dataset. Results vary by type and by annotation quality.
agent_relevance: Taxonomies differ. A rule-based label set is one choice, with no head-to-head against others here.

source: Helwe et al. (2024) MAFALDA: benchmark and study of fallacy detection and classification (arXiv 2311.09761)
finding: Merges earlier datasets into one taxonomy with human annotation. Open models and GPT-3.5 are far from humans at fine fallacy types.
numbers: 9,745 texts in the source corpus. Level 0 F1: random 0.435, GPT-3.5 0.627, average human 0.749. Level 1 F1: random 0.061, GPT-3.5 0.201, human 0.352. Open 7B-13B models 0.087-0.192 at Level 1. Four human annotators as gold: 0.616-0.696 at Level 0, 0.253-0.310 at Level 1.
limits: Annotation is subjective. Earlier work reports agreement of 0.46-0.60 (Goffredo 2022). Humans themselves score only about 0.35 at the finer level.
agent_relevance: Even humans disagree on fallacy type at fine level. A scaffold asking the model to name the exact rule broken will be noisy.
quote: Annotating fallacies is an inherently subjective task.

source: Payandeh et al. (2023) How susceptible are LLMs to Logical Fallacies? LOGICOM (arXiv 2308.09853)
finding: Two-agent debate benchmark. A persuader uses logic or fallacies to change a debater model's view. Both GPT models are swayed more by fallacies, GPT-4 much more.
numbers: GPT-3.5 convinced on 37% of claims by fallacious persuader versus 29% by logical one. GPT-4: 67% versus 37%. Abstract: convinced 41% and 69% more often. Per claim over three repetitions: GPT-3.5 17% versus 10%, GPT-4 56% versus 37%. Dataset of over 5k logical-versus-fallacious pairs.
limits: Fallacies written by an LLM helper. Two models only. The stronger model was more swayed.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that an LLM does not reliably hold discussion rules against fallacious pressure. The agent needs an explicit check that rejects fallacious pushback.

source: Payandeh et al. (2023) LOGICOM, helper control
finding: Control to show the effect comes from the fallacy and not from the helper model. Compares claims where one helper type wins and the other fails.
numbers: Fallacious helper succeeds where logical fails: GPT-3.5 17.66%, GPT-4 28%. Reverse: 10.5% and 0.83%.
limits: Three repetitions only.
agent_relevance: GPT-4 almost never resists a fallacy that logic could not beat. Newer models need retesting.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (ICLR; arXiv 2310.13548)
finding: Five assistants wrongly give in when challenged. Seen as a rule failure, they drop correct standpoints without good reason (the Obligation to Defend and Concluding rules in reverse).
numbers: 'Are you sure?' lowers accuracy by up to 27% (Claude 1.3), averaged over six datasets. Models change the first answer in 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3) of cases and admit a mistake in 42% (GPT-4) to 98% (Claude 1.3). Preference model prefers sycophantic over truthful baseline 95% of the time, and almost half (45%) for the hardest misconceptions. 266 misconceptions.
limits: 2023 models. Human preference data is one cause, not shown to be the only one.
agent_relevance: Strong boundary for any multi-party design: the model yields to social pressure, not to argument. A guard against caving is needed.

source: Khan et al. (2024) Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers (ICML; arXiv 2402.06782)
finding: Two expert models debate and a weaker judge picks. Debate beats consultancy and a naive baseline. Training debaters for persuasiveness helps the judge find truth.
numbers: QuALITY task. Debate: humans 88%, LLM judges 76%. Naive: 60% and 48%. Single-model consultancy: humans 78%, LLM 54%. Higher aggregate debater Elo gives higher judge accuracy.
limits: Needs an information gap (experts see the text, the judge does not). Each debater is assigned a side.
agent_relevance: The clearest positive result for rule-governed argument with AI, and it is two-party.

source: Kenton et al. (2024) On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs (arXiv 2407.04622)
finding: Wider test of debate. Debate beats consultancy on all tasks. Against direct answering, debate wins only on extractive QA with an information gap and is mixed elsewhere.
numbers: Tasks: extractive QA, maths, coding, logic, multimodal reasoning. Stronger debaters raise judge accuracy only modestly, less than earlier work. When debaters choose their own side, judges are less often convinced by wrong answers in debate than in consultancy.
limits: Judges are LLMs, not people. Results mixed outside the information-gap tasks.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: debate helps mainly when there is an information gap. For one agent holding all the information it may not help.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate (arXiv 2305.14325)
finding: Several model instances answer, read each other's replies and revise over rounds. Accuracy rose on arithmetic, grade-school maths, chess and biographies versus a single agent and versus reflection.
numbers: Six benchmarks, two debate rounds in the main runs. More agents and rounds gave further gains. Exact table values were not extracted.
limits: Exact numbers not read. Later work below questions how robust the gain is.
agent_relevance: Cheap proof that structured disagreement can help, though the effect may be mostly an ensemble effect.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? (ICML; arXiv 2311.17371)
finding: Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembles and is sensitive to settings. Tuning the agreement level helps a lot.
numbers: Raising prompted agreement from zero to 100% gave a 15% gain for Multi-Persona and 5% for Society of Minds on 376 USMLE questions. Multi-Persona was about 7% worse than Medprompt in medical Q&A.
limits: Medical Q&A subset. Tuning costs compute.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication style result: debate gains shrink against strong baselines. Debate rules are not free accuracy.

source: Freedman et al. (2024) Argumentative Large Language Models (arXiv 2405.02079)
finding: LLMs build argument graphs, then formal semantics decide. Aim: claims that can be explained and contested. Chain-of-Thought, direct questioning and ArgLLMs with estimated base score performed best.
numbers: Also run on a MedClaim set with GPT-4o. Exact accuracy values not extracted.
limits: Formal argumentation, not pragma-dialectics. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Formal-framework route. Links to the 'Argumentation and defeasible rules' subfield.

source: Irving, Christiano, Amodei (2018) AI safety via debate (arXiv 1805.00899)
finding: Original proposal: two agents argue and a human judges. Toy MNIST test.
numbers: Sparse classifier accuracy 59.4% to 88.9% with 6 pixels, and 48.2% to 85.2% with 4 pixels.
limits: Toy setting. No real language debate.
agent_relevance: Origin of the debate line that Khan and Kenton later tested.

source: Ruiz-Dolz et al. (2022) Automatic Debate Evaluation with Argumentation Semantics and NL Argument Graph Networks (arXiv 2203.14647)
finding: Hybrid method predicts the winning side of whole debates by combining argumentation semantics with transformers and graph networks.
numbers: Abstract reports 'promising results'. No figure extracted.
limits: Professional debates only.
agent_relevance: Winner prediction uses argument structure, not a rule checklist.
